newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Imperial seeks overseas growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Imperial seeks overseas growth.

text.p: Britain's Imperial Tobacco sees good prospects for overseas growth in the face of a declining market for cigarettes in Britain, chief executive Gareth Davis said on Wednesday.
"Our international volumes strengthened despite the strength of sterling and problems with our performance in France, to compensate for that we had increased sales in the southern European countries.
"We see loads of oppurtunities for organic growth on the international side," said Davis.
The company raised its profits from outside Britain by 13 percent to 36 million stg in the half year ended March 29, 1997, comprising 20 percent of total group profits.
Analysts and investors argue that the future of the company depends on its ability to grow profits from overseas as cigarette sales continue to decline in Britain.

Britain's cigarette market has fallen some three percent with Imperial selling less than 15 billion since former Chancellor Kenneth Clarke's November budget which pushed premium cigarette brand prices through three stg a pack.

This also had the effect of forcing many smokers to take up cheaper brands so that Imperial saw an increase in sales of its low price brands under the Lambert & Butler name, which now account for 12 percent of the British market.
British cigarette sales currently amount to about 80 billion a year.

Imperial's French sales were hit by Rothman's launch of Winfield cigarettes, which sell for 22 francs for 30 against Imperial's John Player Special at 16.40 francs for 20, and a government moratorium on any changes to cigarette prices until after the election.
Total sales in France are down some four percent since the government increased duty on cigarettes in December 1996.
Davis said the company would also benefit from greater improvements in production at Dutch cigarette paper maker Rizla, acquired for 185 million stg in January.

He said more efficient production at its main plant in Nottingham will also benefit the group. In Nottingham eight ultra-high speed machines, capable of turning out 14,000 cigarettes every minute, will be installed by the end of the year and workers will move onto a three-shift pattern in a few days.
Davis called on the newly elected Labour government to agree voluntary restrictions on advertising with the tobacco industry rather than imposing a ban by statute.
"If as seems likely there are going to be further restrictions on our marketing freedoms they should be voluntary rather than statutory.

"It is much better done by voluntary means, we have gone into voluntary agreements with government since 1971, with successive curbs on our restrictions. There is already a strong package of restrictions on the cigarette industry."

Davis said it was unclear what the Labour government's pledge to ban all tobacco advertising in Britain meant -- it seemed to include posters and press but possibly not cigarette makers sponsorship of events.
He also argued against any further increase in government tax duty on cigarettes.
"Any further increase in excise taxes is only going to make for more down trading in the UK market and widen the gap in Britain's already punitive excise rate against the rest of Europe."
